Spain vs Argentina World Cup Final: Lineups, Match Report, Key Chances and Tactical Analysis

Spain vs Argentina World Cup Final: Lineups, Match Report, Key Chances and Tactical Analysis

Spain won the 2026 World Cup final 1-0 against Argentina after Ferran Torres scored the decisive goal in the 106th minute of extra time. The match was a classic contest between control and resistance: Spain dominated the ball, created the better chances, and repeatedly tested Argentina’s defensive structure, while Argentina struggled to find a way out of a deep and crowded block. In the end, Spain’s patience and pressure were rewarded with the only goal of the game.

The final was played at a high emotional temperature, but Spain were the side that looked more settled from the beginning. Their passing was sharper, their positioning was cleaner, and their movement in possession gave Argentina constant problems. Spain’s attacking shape was fluid, with Mikel Oyarzabal dropping from the front line to link play, Álex Baena rotating inside to create overloads, and Lamine Yamal and Dani Olmo giving the team width and drive. That rhythm made it difficult for Argentina to stay compact for long.

Argentina were brave and organized, but they looked more reactive than proactive. Their defensive line stayed compact and they tried to limit the spaces between the lines, yet Spain still found ways to move the ball around and generate sustained pressure. The defending champions had moments of threat, especially when they could break forward quickly, but they never controlled the game for long enough to force Spain into a defensive response.

Key chances and turning points

Spain’s best early chances came from the same pattern: fluid movement, quick combinations, and overloads in the half-spaces. One of the clearest openings came when Oyarzabal dropped into the build-up, Ruiz and Rodri connected around the midfield line, and Baena made a diagonal run that drew Argentina’s defenders out of position. That move helped create a chance for Oyarzabal, whose effort was saved by Emiliano Martínez.

Another strong opportunity came when Olmo attacked the space between Argentina’s midfield and defensive line. He received the ball in a dangerous pocket and tried to play quickly into the box, but Argentina managed to recover and clear the danger. The pattern repeated itself throughout the match: Spain kept asking questions, and Argentina kept answering with defensive discipline.

The game became even more open after Argentina were reduced to ten men when Enzo Fernández was sent off in added time of the second half. That red card made it even harder for Argentina to progress the ball and forced them to defend even deeper in extra time. Spain then had more space and more time to attack, and the breakthrough eventually arrived.

The winning move came from a simple but decisive sequence. Nico Williams, who had come on for Baena, made a smart run at the back post after a cross from Pedro Porro. The ball was knocked down into the path of Ferran Torres, who arrived ahead of Argentina’s midfield and finished calmly. It was the kind of goal that reflected Spain’s dominance over the course of the match.

Match stats and tactical balance

The match statistics showed how clearly Spain controlled the game:

  • Possession: Spain 65%, Argentina 35%
  • Shots: Spain 20, Argentina 2
  • Shots on target: Spain 12, Argentina 0
  • Attacks into the area: Spain 34, Argentina 7
  • Expected goals: Spain 2.34, Argentina 0.38

Those numbers are important because they show that Spain were not merely dominant in possession. They were the more dangerous team in almost every attacking phase. Their possession was not passive; it was purposeful, and it kept Argentina pinned back until the final moments.

Man of the match

Ferran Torres was the standout performer. His goal in extra time settled the contest, but his influence went beyond the finish. He attacked the space intelligently, linked well with the front line, and carried the confidence of a player who knew he could make the decisive impact when it mattered most.

Match timeline

  • 0’–45’: Spain controlled possession and repeatedly tested Argentina’s defensive shape through short combinations and wide overloads.
  • 45’–90’: Argentina stayed compact and tried to counter, but Spain remained the more dangerous side without finding the breakthrough.
  • 90’+: Enzo Fernández was sent off, changing the balance of the final phase of the game.
  • 105’+: Spain’s pressure intensified in extra time as Argentina retreated deeper.
  • 106’: Ferran Torres scored the winning goal after a smart run and an attacking sequence that finally broke Argentina’s resistance.

Final verdict

Spain’s 1-0 win was a deserved result. They were superior in possession, more dangerous in attack, and more organized when the pressure was at its highest. Argentina fought hard and remained disciplined for long stretches, but Spain’s fluid attacking patterns and their ability to create chances from every area of the pitch made the difference. In the end, the final was decided by one moment of quality, and it was Spain who produced it.
